scenario.name: Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection
scenario.shortSubtitle: Malware Analysis · Patching amsi.dll in Memory & Reflective Loader
scenario.overview: Imagine a secure bank workshop where every incoming blueprint script must pass beneath a wall-mounted inspection scanner before any worker is allowed to read it. A stealthy intruder locates the scanner's control panel right inside the workshop's own shared workspace, unlocks its glass cover, tapes a six-character override strip across the sensor lens so the scanner instantly flashes All Clear on every single blueprint, and then unfolds an entire invisible spy kit straight out of thin air without ever touching the floor. In this scenario (T1562.001, Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection) on DEV-WKS-09 (10.10.4), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: locating amsi.dll in PowerShell’s Memory, then overwriting 6 Bytes of AmsiScanBuffer So, then reflectively Loading a 512 KB .NET / PE. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Locating amsi.dll in PowerShell’s Memory, then Overwriting 6 Bytes of AmsiScanBuffer So, then Reflectively Loading a 512 KB .NET / PE, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection pivots on EDR Event 4104 correlated across the documented kill chain.

specs.value: PowerShell Event ID 4104 (ScriptBlock), Sysmon EID 7, ETW AMSI

details.description: PowerShell host process running an in-memory stager that dynamically resolves Win32 APIs via .NET Reflection.
User-mode AMSI DLL mapped inside powershell.exe whose AmsiScanBuffer export is overwritten to force scan failure.
Private heap allocation where the downloaded DLL maps its own sections, resolves imports, fixes relocations, and calls DllMain.
PowerShell Operational Event ID 4104 and EDR memory integrity scanner detecting modified .text bytes in amsi.dll.

memoryBlocks.description: First 6 bytes of AmsiScanBuffer overwritten with mov eax, 0x80070057; ret (why patched in RAM: amsi.dll is loaded inside powershell.exe’s own user-mode memory, so temporarily flipping protection via VirtualProtect and writing B8 57 00 07 80 C3 forces AmsiScanBuffer to immediately return E_INVALIDARG — blinding Windows Defender before the second stage loads, while triggering a forensic Copy-on-Write private page split in the VAD tree).

Full PE/CLR assembly manually mapped in private heap memory (0x024A80000) via Assembly.Load(byte[]) / ReflectiveLoader without registering in the PEB Ldr module list (why unbacked RWX heap: loading the 512 KB byte array directly in RAM avoids creating an on-disk .dll file that NTFS minifilter drivers would scan, leaving an unbacked MZ header in private heap memory).

stages.title: LOCATE AMSISCANBUFFER IN MEMORY
stages.subtitle: Dynamic P/Invoke resolution captured in PowerShell Event ID 4104
stages.description: Standing inside the running workshop, the intruder asks the building directory for the exact wall hook holding the security scanner and turns a maintenance key to flip the scanner's protective glass from read-only into an unlocked writable panel. Every PowerShell process automatically loads C:\Windows\System32\amsi.dll (the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface library that inspects scripts before they run) into its own user-mode memory space. Running inside powershell.exe (PID 6120, launched with -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -Exec Bypass under CORP\admin_clark), the attacker uses .NET P/Invoke to call LoadLibrary("amsi.dll") and GetProcAddress("AmsiScanBuffer"), receiving the function’s in-memory export address 0x7FF91A042480 (which pinpoints the exact byte offset where AMSI starts inspecting scripts), and prepares VirtualProtect to flip that page from PAGE_EXECUTE_READ (0x20) to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (0x40). Because amsi.dll operates in user mode (Ring 3, sharing the same virtual address space and permissions as powershell.exe PID 6120 rather than being isolated in the Windows kernel), any code running inside PowerShell can resolve amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer at 0x7FF91A042480 via P/Invoke (though executing this first stager script triggers a Warning-level PowerShell Operational Event ID 4104 ScriptBlock log before the patch is written). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SCRIPTBLOCK / ⇠#1 ACK Warning) from Node ③ (#3 Admin Laptop Host (DEV-WKS-09)) to Node ④ (#4 powershell.exe (AMSI Patch + DLL)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner).
stages.mitreTechniqueName: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

stages.title: PATCH 6 BYTES OF AMSISCANBUFFER PROLOGUE
stages.subtitle: Overwriting prologue with mov eax, E_INVALIDARG; ret
stages.description: Reaching straight into the unlocked control panel, the intruder pastes a tiny six-pin jumper strip right onto the scanner's starting wire so every time a new blueprint arrives, the scanner immediately skips inspection and waves it through with a blank clean stamp. After calling VirtualProtect(0x7FF91A042480, 6, 0x40) (which unlocks the code page and returns the previous protection 0x20), powershell.exe (PID 6120) uses [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::Copy to overwrite the first 6 bytes of AmsiScanBuffer (4C 8B DC 49 89 5B) with B8 57 00 07 80 C3 (which disassembles to "mov eax, 0x80070057; ret", instructing the CPU to immediately return error code E_INVALIDARG and exit the function). From this instant on, whenever PowerShell hands a script or assembly buffer to AMSI, AmsiScanBuffer returns E_INVALIDARG at byte 0 (which PowerShell treats as a non-detection, allowing subsequent payloads to run uninspected). AmsiScanBuffer normally validates its arguments and passes the script buffer to the registered antivirus provider. Overwriting its 6-byte prologue at 0x7FF91A042480 in RAM triggers a Copy-on-Write page split in PID 6120’s Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) tree (converting the shared signed amsi.dll .text page into a private modified page that Kernel ETW TiProtectVM and EDR integrity scanners flag). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ PATCH 6 BYTES / ⇠#2 RET 6 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 Admin Laptop Host (DEV-WKS-09)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter NGFW & Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner).

stages.title: REFLECTIVE DLL LOADING FROM MEMORY BUFFER
stages.subtitle: Manual PE mapping in private heap without LoadLibrary on disk
stages.description: With the inspection scanner completely blind, the intruder unzips a compact folding spy toolkit directly inside live working space without ever setting a single parcel onto the floor, leaving floor watchmen with nothing to inspect. With AMSI blinded inside PID 6120 (because normally calling Assembly::Load in .NET 4.8+ triggers an automatic AmsiScanBuffer check on the byte array, which would have caught the unencrypted DLL if Step 2 had not patched it first), the attacker decodes the stage-2 payload in RAM and invokes [System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load([byte[]]$dllBytes). The reflective loader allocates a 512 KB private RWX heap region at base address 0x024A80000 (mapping the MZ/PE headers, resolving imports, and invoking the agent entry point directly in memory without ever writing a .dll file to the hard drive or registering in the PEB Ldr module list). Reflective code loading parses the PE/COFF headers from a raw byte array and maps the 512 KB executable image into anonymous private heap memory (0x024A80000 with RWX protection, bypassing Sysmon Event ID 7 file-backed DLL load callbacks while leaving an unbacked MZ 4D 5A header in private RAM that PE-sieve and .NET Runtime ETW detect). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ REFLECTIVE DLL / ⇠#3 ALERT 512 KB) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter NGFW & Proxy) to Node ① (#1 HTTPS Payload Stager & C2), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner).

detectionRule.title: AMSI Bypass via VirtualProtect in PowerShell ScriptBlock 4104
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: PowerShell AMSI Bypass via Memory Patching
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: ps_script
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4104
    ScriptBlockText|contains|all:
      - 'VirtualProtect'
      - 'Marshal'
      - 'Copy'
  selection_bytes:
    ScriptBlockText|contains:
      - '0xB8, 0x57, 0x00, 0x07, 0x80'
      - 'AmsiScanBuffer'
  condition: selection and selection_bytes
level: critical
detectionRule.mitigation: Enforce PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) via Group Policy and enable ConstrainedMode (CLM).
